On the order:
First reading of bill to amend and make operative certain provisions of the Copyright Act.-Mr. Ladner.

This bill standing in my name, Mr. Speaker, is one which had its origin in the bill of the hon. senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier), which was introduced on April 1, 1924. As a result of the introduction of that bill and of a further bill dealing with the same subject in 1925, the subject was referred to a special committee, which prepared a report, comprising some three hundred pages, which I have in my hand. The committee went exhaustively into this question, in which the Canadian Authors' Association, the radio people, the theatrical people, and a number of other people in Canada are interested. The committee's report did not seem to find universal approval, and in 1926 I became sponsor for bill No. 3, which was practically a copy of the bill originally introduced by the senior member for Ottawa. Following its introduction, conferences took place between the interested parties, the Canadian Authors' Association, publishers and printers, theatrical and radio people, and as a result a modification of the clauses which were in controversy was agreed to, so that finally the only clause re-

maining which was a matter of controversy was one relating to licenses by which printers and publishers have certain rights in regard to reproducing works in Canada against the wishes of the authors of these works.
In 1927, by Bill No. 45, the subject was again introduced into parliament, but through the exigencies of parliamentary business and procedure, that measure was never carried through to completion, and now this bill stands on the order paper in my name for presentation to parliament this year.
I wish to explain that I understand from a statement which the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) made to the house the other day, that it is not the intention of the government to introduce a measure relative to the Copyright Act this session. I believe also that a convention is being held in Rome at *which it is hoped by most of us, and indeed it is likely, a representative of Canada will be present. That convention has to deal with matters in connection with the Berne convention, of which Canada along with thirty-five other nations is a member, and as a result of international rearrangements regarding copyright which may be made at that convention, I am hoping that the government will see its way clear to introduce a measure providing a remedy that will satisfy the claims of the authors, as well as certain other remedies which certainly ought to ibe provided by parliament. I shall not enter into details at this stage because they are well known to the government. As I have reason to believe that the government will, following this convention in Rome, introduce a measure to remedy the situation, and perhaps considerably revise the Copyright Act, I ask leave to withdraw this bill.
Bill withdrawn.

The house resumed, from April 18, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution. - Mr. Cardin. - Mr. Johnston in the chair:
That it is expedient to authorize a loan 'o the harbour commissioners of Quebec in - r. amount not exceeding $8,500,000 to carry on

Quebec Harbour Commission
the construction of terminal facilities, upon approval by the governor in council of detailed plans, specifications and estimates for such works, and the deposit of debentures of the corporation to cover said loan.

Some few
years ago this house had before it a vote of a similar character. At that time the amount asked for was $5,000,000 and the minister in response to queries stated that the $5,000,000 was to cover a five-year program. Moreover, >'e said that this was all that would be required for that program. According to his statement, that five-year program will not have reached its conclusion until 1930; yet we find the government coming back to the house again this year and asking for $8,500,000 more. At that time it was demonstrated to the satisfaction of the committee that the facilities at Quebec were ample for the business then being transacted-absolutely ample. A considerable opposition from this corner of the house, and some from my friends to the right, has arisen on the ground of the nonnecessity for this expenditure, and the suggestion has been made that the item might be laid over until such time as the traffic flow into Quebec will have shown a sufficient increase in volume to justify the additional facilities asked for. These facilities at the time of the previous vote were not required, but it was explained by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) as well as by the Minister of Marine (Mr. Cardin) that if they were provided the business would go to the port. It was also indicated that within a short time it was expected that the grain rate from Armstrong to Quebec would be reduced. Now that grain rate has been reduced; it has been cut almost in two. Yet the total increase has been but 5,000,000 bushels. At that time about 5,000,000 bushels went through the port, and the total last year was about 10,000,000. According to the minister's own admission also the capacity of the elevator will not be reached until 40,000.000 bushels per season passes through the port.
I have visited the port and have seen the docks down there and I must compliment Quebec and this government on the excellent facilities they have provided for cattle. I do not think that an hon. member opposite will allege for a moment that there is any further space required for cattle storage. The question arose yesterday regarding deep sea vessels, liners and so forth, and there was some half-hearted interjection to the .effect that the amount of money asked for was required to make it possible for more of these

larger vessels to dock. I do not know why that statement should have been made. I myself have inspected one of the largest liners afloat, the Empress of Scotland, which was docked at Quebec; and we all know that many of the other great transatlantic liners dock there frequently.
Frankly I am not prepared at this moment definitely to oppose this vote. If forced to do so I will vote against this resolution, unless the government is prepared to allow the bill which will follow to go before a committee where we can get information from the engineers, examine the blue prints, and have a full demonstration of the requirements of the port, together with proof of the prospects of an increased volume of business. The request is not an unreasonable one. I admit it is not original; the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) made it yesterday, and it was supported by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence). The minister will find that most hon. members on this side of the house will be perfectly willing to pass this resolution if he will agree to send the bill to a committee for further examination. It is perfectly absurd to expect us to let the matter go through at this stage when we take into consideration the weak response the minister has so far been able to make to the request for information as to the necessity for this vote. His explanation has been so futile as to convince me that until we have further information this house would not be justified in passing the resolution. If the minister desires to have the resolution go through, let him undertake to send the bill to a committee. Not only would he be wise in doing so, but he would be showing confidence in his own view of the matter. He would be saying to the house, virtually, "We have nothing to hide; this matter is open and aboveboard. The facilities are needed and we are prepared to prove it." But he has not yet proved his case. Indeed, I do not think the government can prove it in this house, and all we ask is that we be given an opportunity to get the facts. We have a right to ask this before we are urged to vote this enormous sum of money, at least two years before the program of 1925 is completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It was not my intention to speak at this stage, expecting to make, on the second reading of the bill, any remarks I have to offer. But there have been such extraordinary statements in the course of the discussion that I think I owe it to those I represent in this parliament to say something now. In the first place, this amount which is

Quebec Harbour Commission
asked for in connection with Quebec harbour comprises two items. One is to complete the Wolfe's cove harbour development, started after the appropriations of 1925. This item would be $5,310,000. The second item is for new grain and other facilities on the Louise docks-that is, the old harbour. It amounts to $2,840,000. There are also debentures issued to the public amounting to $350,000 which fall due in 1928 and 1929, and these must be met. These are the items which make up the amount of $8,500,000.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would prefer to finish my statement.
I want to get this clearly in my mind. Is the wharf at Wolfe's cove the same wharf for which $2,800,000 was voted in 1925?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: But of that amount $2,800,000 was for one wharf. Is this the same wharf?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The whole $5,000,000 was for the improvement of Wolfe's cove. I am going to show my hon. friend the work which has been done, if he will allow me to proceed with my explanation.
The reasons given to the house in 1925 were that the old harbour was not sufficient for the traffic which was using the port of Quebec. Obviously the new works, which are not completed, cannot be utilized at present, and there were then and still are seven deepwater berths provided with shed accommodation in that harbour. Three of these berths weTe used and are being used by ships which carry immigrants, and these berths cannot be rented or leased to shipping companies; they must be available all the time for ships carrying passengers and immigrants. One of these sheds has been burned since 1925, and part of the money which is asked for is to provide for the reconstruction of that shed. Last year only two berths were available for passenger and immigrant traffic, and many ships were detained through lack of accommodation. Two other berths are used for ordinary cargoes such as lumber, cement, asbestos and so on, as well as for cattle. Facilities to take care of that traffic have been built in recent years, and obviously those two berths cannot be used for passengers or immigrants. One berth, number four, is rented to the Canadian Pacific Steamship Company, while two other berths are used for grain and for oil bunkers; these are used to their full capacity. One berth
is rented to one of the shipping companies;
I do not know whether it is the Cunard or another line. Those are the only berths available, and as I have already said three of them are used for the immigrant and passenger traffic.
A few moments ago my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) handed me a telegram from the secretary-treasurer of the harbour board indicating what space is used for the immigrant traffic. It is as follows:
Total frontage Quebec for ocean vessels 8,150 lineal feet not including coasting berths. Frontage taken up by immigrants, passenger boats at berths 18. 26, 28 and 29, 3,300 lineal feet, or 40 per cent.
That is the reason why the shipping federation petitioned the government, stating that additional facilities were required there. The president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the head of the Canadian National Railways both endorsed the demands then made upon the government for the extension of the harbour, as being a work winch was absolutely necessary.
What has been done? At the time the last vote was passed much opposition was manifested, really more than the bill deserved. The works at Wolfe's Cove were started immediately afterwards, during the navigation season of 1925, and they have progressed satisfactorily during the years 1926 and 1927. Sixteen cribs, having a total length of 2,666 feet, are now sunk in position and filled with stone, and the concrete superstructure on top of these cribs was to have been started early in this year. It is expected that by the close of navigation this year this wharf surface will be completed. The remaining cribs for a length of 1,634 feet, to complete the 4.300 feet of wharf, must be sunk in 1928, as one year must elapse after they are sunk to allow the concrete wall to be erected thereon. The present application for a vote of $5,310,000, which is a necessary complement to the first application, includes the construction of the necessary facilities and equipment without which the wharves cannot be utilized by the shipping interests. When the wharf is completed the facilities to be erected thereon such as sheds, railway tracks, elevators and so forth, are all works which can and must be executed at the same time in order to have these facilities ready for operation with the least possible delay. Some of my hon. friends opposite were asking yesterday why the previous vote of $5,000,000 had not produced any revenue as yet. It cannot produce any revenue until the work is completed; it is easy to see that. Shipping companies have made application for space in the new har-

Quebec Harbour Commission
bour, as sooa as the work is completed. The works which have been begun with the vote of $5,000,000 cannot remain as they are; they must be completed.
The second item is for enlarging the grain elevator and for some other works which are necessary in the old harbour. In 1925, when the question of the shipment of grain through the port of Quebec was discussed in this house, hon. gentlemen opposite of the Progressive group took the position that it was absurd to provide for that movement, because a prohibitive rate was in force on the Transcontinental Railway, and that railway was not serving the purpose for which it was built. I admitted at that time that the claim was sound in many respects. I admit that my hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) has been a consistent advocate of the use of the port of Quebec for the shipment of grain. He argued that the rates should be decreased; that it was of vital importance and even a necessity that the port of Quebec should be used for the shipment of grain. Well, I promised at that time that I would use all my energy for the purpose of trying to reach that desirable goal. I think we have succeeded. Much work has been done, and finally we were pleased to have the railway board of Canada decide that the rate had to be decreased. It was decreased and is now 11 cents and as a result, as I said yesterday, the harbour commissioners report that the elevator has been filled since the reduced rate went into force. But those who wish to see the desired goal reached, state that it will be useless to have the rate decreased unless the facilities in the port are also extended. That statement is made in the report of the Royal Commission on Grain. That was not urged by the people of Quebec; that was not the statement of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) or of the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) or of myself. The Royal Commission on Grain said that the storage and elevator facilities in the port of Quebec should be largely extended. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) read a letter yesterday from a man who is deeply interested in the grain trade, Mr. Smith-I think he is one of the officers of the pool-saying that these improvements are necessary, and that shippers cannot take full advantage of the reduced rate unless the needed facilities are provided.
One hon. member who spoke yesterday said that the west is not asking for these improvements and facilities and that they will be a charge upon that part of Canada. Well,

I do not think that is a fair argument. As I said, all those bodies which have urged these improvements are not animated by a local point of view. The commission referred to, for example, was appointed to study the problems in connection with the grain trade and they suggested that this work be done. Furthermore, I have in my hand a petition signed by members and senators representing western constituencies, dated September 25, 1920, and addressed to Sir Robert Borden, then Prime Minister of Canada. No Quebec name appears on that petition. I am not a signatory of it. I did not know at the time that such a petition had been drawn up and signed. But in that petition the very improvements which we are proposing to-day were asked for and suggested by these western members and senators. I will read only the last portion of the petition to the following effect:
That it make such arrangements that the marine insurance rates from Canadian seaports shall be the same as from New York, and that sufficient additional grain storage be built at Quebec, Halifax and St. John to handle the business in Canadian grain which, we believe, it will be possible to win back from New York, if these suggestions are adopted.
These are the final words of the petition that was signed and addressed to Sir Robert Borden in 1920 not by the Quebec members but by the western members of the House of Commons and of the senate.
Now the trouble we are experiencing is due to the fact that the work is being done under a commission. But we are not responsible for that. The present commission system now in force in regard to the harbour of Quebec was instituted in 1913. Somebody said yesterday:	Surely the commissioners must have
been lacking in competence to have allowed matters to go on as they did. I think I need only mention the names of those who have been at the head of the board to show that those men did their best. Certainly they were men who enjoyed the confidence not only of the community of Quebec but of Canada as a whole. My hon. friends opposite will remember Sir William Price. Surely that man stood high in the estimation of the people of Canada and his memory has been held in general esteem since his death. Sir William Price was a former chairman of the Quebec harbour board. He is one of those who were responsible for the starting of the work at Quebec, and he always claimed that it was impossible for the commission to take interest because the best part of the harbour is used for government purposes and in the national interest. Then we had

Quebec Harbour Commission
Senator L'Esperance. He is one of the able members of the senate who has been president of the harbour commission. Ask Senator L'Esperance about these improvements. He devoted his time and his energy to carrying out the works projected for the harbour. We have had the late General Sir David Watson, who distinguished himself in the war. He was a president of the Quebec harbour commission and a first class man. I may say that the present president of the Quebec harbour commission, the Hon. Mr. Power, possesses the confidence of all the citizens of the district irrespective of politics, and is doing his best in the interests of the harbour. But as I said 40 per cent of the best part of the harbour is used for national interests and is absolutely unproductive as far as the work of the board is concerned. The commission have tried to remedy that condition, just as their predecessors did. They claim that the most important of the facilities at Quebec harbour are for passengers and for immigrants. The commissioners sought to bring about a remedy and they passed a by-law' with that object in view, but every by-law which the board passes has to be accepted by the government. The commission are not as free in that respect as any other financial institution would be. They adopted a by-law to impose a charge of a dollar per head upon every person using the port of Quebec or landing there. There is nothing extraordinary in that. It is done in other ports, not in Canada, but in the ports of other countries. The port of Cherbourg is one of the important ports of France, and it has been built up and developed in that way. I have disembarked and embarked at the port of Cherbourg and I have been charged a tax for doing so. But the government has always taken the position that it would hurt immigration to Canada if such a charge were to be imposed. The claim has been made also that the steamship companies would have to pay the toll and incorporate it in their passenger rates. But successive governments and departments of immigration at Ottawa have always held that we should abstain from such a course in order to encourage immigration. Very well, I do not object to that, but it makes the facilities at Quebec public works in the interest of the country at large. The system was again ratified by parliament when last year we adopted legislation for the purpose of putting both Halifax and St. John under the control of commissions. These two ports will now be coming to parliament asking for advances; it is the only way by which they can do their work, and there is no way of avoiding it.

In my opinion-and I speak merely as a practical grain man who has had something to do with the business in a rather large way-there are great possibilities in the accommodation of the cheapest kind of grain storage at the port of Quebec in order to enable those interested in the grain business to utilize the low rate which now exists and to accumulate their grain at that point near the seaboard for export as soon as the season opens in the spring.
I have only one other word to say, and that is with reference to the statement of the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell). I understood him to say, with reference to the Hudson Bay route, that it was in the nature of a political bribe to the people of the west. If I am unfair in my understanding of what he said I hope he will correct me now. I want to contradict that statement;
I only hope my hon. friend was not bribed by it; because I would consider the price altogether too high.

I do not profess to have
the experience with regard to the storage of grain which is possessed by the Minister of Railways, but from such knowledge as I have of the operations of the port of Montreal I think I can say that the earnings of that port are larger during the summer months, when grain is being transhipped, than during the winter months when the elevators are used for storage purposes. I think there is no doubt about that.

I wish my hon. friend
would repeat that statement; I did not catch it.

I think the earnings per
month of the elevators in the port of Montreal are larger during those months when the port is open to navigation than when these elevators are used simply for storage purposes. My hon. friend shakes his head. I will have the figures looked up, and we will have an opportunity to discuss that question later. I wish the minister had refreshed his memory before making such a positive statement as he has made.

I would not argue that
in connection with the port of Montreal they do not have tremendous earnings simply out of the transfer business, but the winter storage in Montreal is clear profit, with no expenses attached to it.

That is an entirely different issue, and places a different complexion on the statement which I understood the minister to make.
Some reference has been made to Vancouver. I do not think any hon. member of this house who has watched the progress of that port can fail to have a feeling of satisfaction and pride in the way Vancouver has developed. Of course it has the advantage of being on the Pacific coast; it is open during the whole year. Sometimes I think that if Columbus had only discovered the Pacific coast of America before he discovered the Atlantic coast the development on the Pacific coast would have been beyond the reach of our imagination. On our north Atlantic coast, of course, we have severe winters; many of our ports along the St. Lawrence are closed for a considerable part of the year, and the earnings of those ports are seriously diminished as compared with the earnings of the ports on the Pacific coast.
With regard to the port of Quebec, I do not believe any member of this house has any objection to the development of that port in the national interest of Canada. If I felt that we as a party opposed the development

Quebec Harbour Commission
of that great port-and it will be a great port in the future-I would have to dissent absolutely from that view. However, I look upon Quebec as a port which is likely to be open all year within the next ten or fifteen years; I sincerely hope that such developments in the navigation of the St. Lawrence to Quebec may be made as to render it possible to keep that port open for at least ten months of the year. Having that possibility in mind, I believe the members of this house are desirous that this port should have every facility which is required for its future development.
However, there is a difficulty in the way. Personally I do not think the traffic of the port of Quebec, which at present is largely a passenger traffic, can be properly developed if it is anticipated that that port will pay the carrying charges on the money necessarily invested in its development. Therefore personally I am opposed to the commission system as applied to these eastern ports with which I am more or less familiar. The Minister o-f Justice hardly met the criticism which has been made from this side erf the house; at least I put a different interpretation upon that criticism than the one which the minister has placed. If the government had come to the house and asked for an appropriation of so many million dollars, five or eight as the case may be, for the purpose of developing the port of Quebec as a national port, without any subterfuge whatsoever, I feel that his proposal would have met with more general approval. This appropriation is presented as a loan, and that is a mere subterfuge. There is no anticipation that the development of trade and commerce in the port of Quebec, which at present consists largely of immigration and regular passenger services with such additional traffic as comes through it in the way of freight will, within a reasonable term of years, create sufficient revenue to pay the interest upon the advances necessary, or for return of the principal or provide for the depreciation of property in the meantime. That being so, why keep up this subterfuge? Why set forth upon the statute books of Canada that you are making a loan to the harbour commission for which you are receiving its debentures upon which interest is payable annually, when there is no reasonable prospect of the port having sufficient revenue to repay to the government the interest and sinking fund on that loan.
That is the criticism which I make with regard to placing such harbours as Chicoutimi, St. John, and Halifax under commissions which receive loans from the Dominion government and are expected to pay the interest on these loans and sinking funds, plus the depreciation of harbour works, from the receipts obtainable from t'he traffic entering those ports. I suggest that putting Halifax, for instance, under a commission with t'he expectation that that commission will be able to tax the trade of Halifax harbour to a sufficient amount to repay the principal and interest of the loans necessary for t'he development of that port is perfectly futile-nay, it is ridiculous. If that port, placed under a commission, is to be taxed a sufficient amount to repay interest plus the cost of operation and sinking fund for repayment of principal, the tax upon the shipping of that port would be so great as to prevent any trade or commerce entering from the Atlantic. And in the case of the port of St. John, for its commission to assume so large a capital indebtedness is one of the measures which will retard the development of the trade and commerce of the port rather than develop it, because it will necessitate placing such a tax upon the trade directly passing through that port as to preclude the port from fulfilling its functions as a great national outlet and inlet. Therefore T suggest that with regard to certain classes of ports which are really parts of our national transportation system, and which are as neces-sarjr to transportation as the railways of the country and without which the railways could not function efficiently, they should be regarded as national ports to be sustained by the national government, and that we should not resort to the trick and subterfuge of making advances or loans for the developments of these ports, when the trade and traffic will not give a revenue sufficient to maintain operations and pay sinking funds and interest thereon.
If the government will examine into these eastern ports along the St. Lawrence which are only open for traffic for a limited season of the year, and if it will look into the trade-and traffic passing through Halifax and St.. John it will find that it will be absolutely impracticable for these ports to earn sufficient to pay their way. Why then go through the farce of making loans which are really cash advances the repayment of which you may never reasonably expect? That is the measure of criticism which I have to make. The port of Montreal is so far paying the interest upon the advances made. It is having some difficulty in keeping up the sinking fund for the payment in the future of its bonds as they become due; and in the case of that port if you are to tax its trade sufficiently to obtain a return to the country of the principal and

Quebec Harbour Commission
interest, plus the carrying charges of the (port, you will soon have to impose such taxation upon the trade passing through Montreal as to preclude it from really ever functioning as a national port of Canada. I do not like to do things by way of pretext or by subterfuge. Personally I do not like following an ancient practice or a practice which has been established by other governments before the present administration, and to offer the procedure formerly followed as a justification for continuing to make these loans.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps we are the true
Conservatives in that respect.

I have found the province
of Quebec to be more Conservative than it receives credit for. My hon. friend who is so critical of precedents at times, is always willing to justify his own conduct by some far-fetched precedent from a Conservative regime.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is in order that my
argument shall have greater influence upon those to whom it is addressed.

If my hon. friend would
address himself to the actual facts and the actual conditions that prevail rather than to devising fallacious arguments to appeal to the intellects on this side, his speeches oftentimes would be more effective than they are.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear.

But to state my case briefly: It goes against the grain, coming as I do from the province of Quebec, to take an adverse stand, but I would point out that never will a single measure come before the house which I regard as justifiable in the interests of the country as a whole, while at the same time calculated to promote the development of these ports of Quebec but it will receive my earnest support. But it goes against the grain to vote for a loan of S8.500,-000 when I know it is essentially not a loan, but that some day in some way some offset must be found for that unless the harbour commission of Quebec is to acknowledge itself bankrupt. If that commission is to be maintained as a commission, an appropriation should be made to it annually for providing facilities for the immigration service which is carried on though the port of Quebec and which is essential to the well-being and development of the whole of Canada. In the second place, apart from the freight traffic, if it is desirable that we should develop the passenger traffic at that port as a great inlet and outlet for both national railways, we

should consider making a further appropriation in that respect so as to relieve the city of Quebec of the burden of carrying locally the charges for what is really a great national undertaking and one absolutely necessary not only for the development of the commerce of the country but to preserve for all time commercial outlets and inlets for our export and import business.
Further, with regard to that part of the works which may be developed and which are used in the ordinary course by the steamship companies making their headquarters at Quebec, they should pay a reasonable amount as well for these facilities. What I object to is the futility of placing upon Quebec the burden of alone maintaining these great national services out of the taxable traffic which passes through that port. I do not think Quebec can carry that Ipurden alone. The whole matter should be reconsidered. When I am saying that I am not disparaging the city of Quebec. We have, as the Minister of Railways has said, given certain facilities to trade and traffic as far as Montreal. We undoubtedly will in future provide facilities for trade and traffic far beyond Montreal into the interior as this country grows and develops. But Quebec, to my mind, looking to the future, will become a great ocean port which is bound to carry a large part of the trade and traffic of eastern Canada not only during what we now term the summer and autumn season, but throughout at least ten or eleven . months of the year. Therefore I am anxious to see this port developed; but I commend to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and to other hon. gentlemen who represent Quebec in the government that they should consider meeting the problem fairly and fully now, and that they should not year by year place upon the port of Quebec a financial burden in respect of which the trade and traffic of that city alone will never be able to make a sufficient return to meet the obligations of the Harbour Commission.

The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was evidently somewhat annoyed at remarks which I made the other day, because he brought up the Welland canal as being on a par with this development at Quebec. First of all I wish to point out to him, although he knows it quite well, that the Welland canal is not under the commission but under parliament. The work is being performed by government engineers and each year the accounts come before the department and we have an opportunity of discussing the estimates in the house. There is a great deal of difference between that method of procedure and a commission coming to par-

Quebec Harbour Commission
liamen.t and asking for a five-year cheque without any regard being had, so fair as the house is concerned, to how the money is to be spent, and ail we have is an audit that, if any atention were paid to it, might induce members to vote differently from the way they have done in the past. When the question was before parliament in 1925 I never spoke on it at all. I was prepared to sit and listen to the information that was given in regard to the situation. Apparently the fact that I quoted the minister's own statement also annoyed the Minister of Justice. Because I quoted from 1925 the statement of the then and the present minister he did not like it. Was that because it was true? On t-hait occasion I listened to the members who spoke on the subject and I voted on the question because of the arguments brought forward by those who were providing the goods to go through the port. I refer to Mr. Sales, the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and others of those who knew. I refer also to the minister who is sitting right in front of me, the present Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke). I do not recollect that he said anything on the question but I know I voted the way he did. The hon. member for Pro-vencher (Mr. Beaubien) also made a long address. I voted then against the motion while he also voted against it, and I presume he and others will vote against this further advance because this is worse than the last one.

I have received a good
deal of information since that time.

The hon. member may
have received something more than information. Perhaps he will give us the information. For the benefit of those who probably did not care to look up what happened several years ago. I want to quote again what was said when the matter came up in 1925. Mr. Caldwell, who was opposing the vote, asked the minister the following question:
Mr. Caldwell:	Could the minister tell us
what amount of grain the present facilities at Quebec could handle yearly if used to their full capacity?
Those are not, as the Minister of Justice says, the facilities that are being built now or that were being built last year, but the facilities that were in existence in 1925. As regards the facilities that were in existence then, the minister gives this reply:
Mr. Cardin:	I am told it is forty million
bushels.
That was the capacity then, and what has been the result? Ten million bushels of grain have passed through that port. They have
not done more business than that with a forty million bushel capacity and yet they are coming to parliament requesting a larger vote to provide even greater facilities. According to the minister's own statement, the facilities for wheat or other grain are four times as great as they have required.
What is said about the facilities for cattle? They have built large facilities for cattle. With the facilities which were then in existence ten thousand head of cattle could be handled, yet during one year I think the number reached five thousand and the average prior to the present year has not been more than three thousand. Indeed the number went as low as 1,500 head of cattle during one year.
In respect to the Montreal development someone said that by developing Montreal we hurt Quebec. Was it wrong to have developed the port of Montreal? Was the money expended on the port of Montreal money wrongly spent? If the money was properly spent in Montreal, must we now go back and subsidize Quebec to make it as cheap a port as Montreal? If it is cheaper to carry goods to Montreal, that is where they will be carried. I have nothing against the port of Quebec. I want to see all our ports provided with the necessary facilities to carry the traffic that is coming to them, but certainly it has not been demonstrated that Quebec is a cheap port to run, and, of course, the traffic will go where the charges are the lowest.
The minister criticized a remark I made about the western people building an elevator in Buffalo. The remark I made was quite apropos. If those people will go into a port like Buffalo, where grain can be handled cheaper, and will build there an elevator without any cost to the country at all, why should we have to build elevators ourselves in Quebec or any other port if private interests will do it? It must mean that grain can be handled cheaper through Buffalo than through Quebec. The minister told us in 1925 that Quebec had a capacity of forty million bushels, and yet in only one year has it handled ten million bushels; in the other years it has handled only about five million bushels. Therefore, until Quebec is using approximately up to the capacity it has, I do not see why we should spend money to provide further capacity that may never be used.

I had no intention of
taking part in this discussion because I was not in the house yesterday, and I had not given any particular study to the question, but some of the comparisons which the Minister of Justice made were so malapropos that I just wish to mention one or two of them. He said,

Quebec Harbour Commission
for instance, that something like thirteen or fourteen million dollars had been spent on the harbours of Fort William and Port Arthur, which is really one harbour. But the difference is this. While the port of Quebec handled last year something under ten million bushels, Fort William and Port Arthur handled nearly three hundred million bushels, and while the port of Quebec has had over seventeen million dollars expended on it, which with this eight and one-half millions will make over twenty-five millions, about half that amount has been expended on Fort William and Port Arthur, handling the immense amount of grain they do, as well as general freight.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are other sources
of traffic than grain. Over one hundred thousand immigrants came to Quebec last year, and not one to Fort William.

I venture to make the assertion that nearly as many immigrants came through Fort William and Port Arthur as through Quebec, and it must be remembered that these immigrants do not stop at Quebec; they pass through.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But they do not land at Fort William.

No, but it does not require an expenditure of twenty-five million dollars to prepare the port of Quebec for the landing of immigrants. I was saying that in spite of the vast amount of grain that is handled at the head of the lakes, making Port Arthur and Fort William the greatest grain-shipping port, I believe, in the world, the expenditure on that port is just about half of what will have been expended on the port of Quebec when the sum mentioned here is expended.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not opposed to expenditure at Fort William.

Nor am I opposed to expenditures at the port of Quebec so long as the work is really requited. The port of Vancouver in 1923 had less than two million bushels elevator capacity, and yet in that year it handled fifty million bushels. It is true that it has not handled so much since then, but with a capacity of two million bushels it handled in one year fifty million bushels.
I think the point made by the hon. member for Lincoln a few minutes ago was sound, and that is that if there is a demand for additional elevator capacity at any port, generally speaking you will find private interests who will be glad to provide the capacity. Nearly all the elevators at the head of the

lakes, except one large one, were built by private funds, and I believe that if greater facilities are needed at the port of Quebec, there will be private interests who will be glad to provide them.
I did not rise for the purpose of opposing the expenditure on the port o.f Quebec because, like anybody else who has visited it, I love the old city of Quebec. I think anyone who has any sentiment in him cannot come away from that city without a real affection for it, but it is the duty of parliament to scrutinize the expenditures that are made at any port and in any part of Canada. Unfortunately, with this harbour commission form of government, we do not get the opportunity of scrutinizing the expenditures at the port. There are many people in the city of Quebec, I believe, who do not think these improvements are necessary. I was there some time ago myself, and while naturally I do not wish to mention names, there were many citizens of Quebec who told me that the expenditures were a long distance ahead of the necessities of the port, and they told me also that the expenditures were made so carelessly that perhaps they were made for other purposes than the building up of the port of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wish these informers
would say that to me. I have never met one who would say such a thing.

If they did, my hon. friend would not repeat it in the house. I stand by my hon. friend in supporting the expenditure in Quebec, and by the hon. gentleman behind him (Mr. Power), for whom I have always a friendly feeling. I understand that he is supporting this vote just as I would support a vote for any work that I considered necessary at Fort William or Port Arthur, but I think the government would be well advised to allow all these expenditures to be properly investigated by this house, or if not by this house, by some committee of this house, with the right to call before them the commissioners of the port of Quebec, and go thoroughly into the expenditures which are being made in the port. I do not wish to .take the attitude of opposing an expenditure like this, but in view of the comparatively small traffic passing through the port of Quebec, as compared with other ports mentioned by the Minister of Justice, I find it difficult to understand why so mucih money is needed, and much more difficult to understand why we should not have all these expenditures thoroughly scrutinized, whether they are made in the port of Quebec or elsewhere.

Quebec Harbour Commission

I would not have taken
part in this debate had not the Minister of Justice seen fit to refer to the good city of Toronto. He well knows my feelings with regard to the national port of Quebec. I had the honour and privilege of saying a few words in this house on behalf of the city of Quebec when the minister was in his seat, and he was gracious enough to congratulate me afterwards on the good word I had said for Quebec. It is, however, very disappointing to us to see the slow progress which the port of Quebec is making not only in the handling of grain, but also in the handling of live cattle and hay. When the $5,000,000 loan to Quebec harbour was under consideration in 1925, it was stated that a great movement of cattle and of hay and of grain could be expected through the port of Quebec, but the facts adduced as to those movements are not such as to warrant this house in voting another $8,500,000 for the port, and before we go ahead in an experimental way and spend this large amount of money, I think we should be shown what results have been achieved by the expenditure of the $5,000,000 loan voted in 1925. Before asking us to vote this money, you should demonstrate to us that the port of Quebec is developing as fast as you were wont to prophesy it would when in 1925 you obtained a vote of $5,000,000 for the port.
It has been my privilege during the past five years never to miss an opportunity of passing a day in Montreal and two or three weeks in Quebec. The Minister of Justice will admit that Quebec is not going ahead in point of population and industry or as a national port at the same rate as some of our other ports. In regard to port development, I have in mind particularly Montreal; in regard to growth of population and industrial development I am thinking of the city of Toronto. And may I refer to the manner in which the Minister of Justice mentioned the city of Toronto? His heated tone and wild gesture rather amused me, and' I did not think he was helping to improve the bonne entente between the two 'provinces. The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Cas-grain), the government whip, interjected something about Scarborough beach. Let me tell the house that not one dollar of the money of this Dominion has ever been spent on protection of the Scarborough beach area. It is not covered by the 1913 agreement. In that area which I have the honour to represent there are 100,000 good Canadian citizens, and they deserve some consideration at the hands -of the government. The hon. gentleman's interjection was most inept. I may
say that the city of Toronto is standing behind the Toronto harbour commission in paying badk the bulk of the loss which has been sustained, in order that the harbour may be developed and' that loss 'in years to come converted into an asset not only for the city of Toronto but for the whole Dominion. As every hon. member knows, it is the duty of the Dominion government to protect the shore line where there are large centres of population. Under the 1913 agreement the Toronto shore line protection work from Woodbine avenue west is being assisted by the Dominion government, but not eastward in 'the Scarborough area, where, as I said, there is a population of 100,000 To-day the city of Toronto has been generous enough to advance the necessary funds to protect the shore line, and up to the present the Dominion government has not been asked to participate in the cost, although, I repeat, it is the duty of the federal authorities to look after this work. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries will admit that the city of Quebec is very fortunate in that the rock formation resists the ravages of storms much better than the sandy shore line of Toronto.
Now, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries should give us some more details as to what has been done at the port of Quebec during the past three years. What about the shipments of hay, cattle and wheat from the port,? What has been the development along the line voiced in this house by many hon. members in 1925-encouraging more and more traffic over the transconitinental line? Let the minister give us facts and figures so that we may vote intelligently on this proposal, and let those facts and figures bear some relationship to the experiment which we undertook in 1925 when we voted $5,000,000 in order that a national port might be developed at Quebec. It might be edifying to hear the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) and other of our Progressive friends reiterate some of the statements they made in 1925 in support of the vote to which I have referred, but they are sitting very quiet to-day-there has been an election or two in the intervening years. I was sorry to see the Minister of Justice rise to such great heights of eloquence in an attempt to introduce political issues. Instead of anting as a statesman and giving us information on which we might base an intelligent decision, he told us what we had done years before. Let me tell him that the people of this country are tired of politics; they want to hear sound business arguments. As the matter stands now, I do not feel disposed to vote in favour of the proposed loan. I would urge the government to use a little

Quebec Harbour Commission
common sense and refer the proposal to a committee, for conclusive facts and figures to be submitted. In 1925 we were promised that, given, lower freight rates, there would be such a 'movement of grain through the port of Quebec that the interest and other charges would be fully met. Well, the freight rates have been lowered, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has had an opportunity to tell us haw the business of the port has developed.. Let him now tell us why he is asking for another $8,500,000. Let him base his request on the facts and figures which he must have under his hand at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that whatever facts and figures I might quote to my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Harris) they would not satisfy him, and he would ask for still further information before admitting that this request is absolutely justified.
I should like the hon. minister to base that assertion on facts too.

There is one point which
does not seem to be very clear in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite. It is the expenditure made out of the vote of $5,000,000 authorized in 1925. As I think I explained at the opening of the discussion, this amount has not been all spent. Work has been started at Wolfe's Cove, the new terminal, but it is not yet completed. About two and a half or three million dollars has been spent' in the building of cribs and the dredging necessary for the placing of these cribs, as well as for other materials essential to the completion of the work. The contractors have already sunk sixteen cribs, and the work on the top of the cribs cannot be completed before a certain period has elapsed to permit the proper footing of the cribs. It takes two years before the cribs can be properly sunk, and before you can begin building the concrete superstructure. The work, I say, has been started and cannot be completed before the end of this year. By the end of the summer season of 1928 the work in connection with nearly the whole of the $5,000,000 will have been finished.
There are certain works to be provided for. We have to provide sheds, rails and other facilities on these new wharves which are being constructed, and we come before parliament this year for the reason that we do not wish to run short of money at the end of next year before we can complete the work already started. At the end of the navigation season of 1928, I repeat, certain work I have outlined will be completed. If we have no money available to complete the work at this

terminal we shall be exposed to delays, and we decided therefore that it would be preferable to come this year before parliament, before the $5,000,000 has been completely expended, in order to get the necessary funds to carry on profitably.
We have no return to show on the money
already expended, for the very good reason given by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and myself yesterday: these works are not completed and therefore cannot be utilized. At the present time the work consists merely in cribs which have been sunk and filled with stone, and a certain amount of dredging has been done. We cannot use the cribs to advantage as they stand. We need the money we are asking for if we are to complete the work, but it will not take the full $8,500,000. The amount necessary to complete the wharves, tracks, sheds and elevator facilities is $5,300,000, and the other sums contributing to, the total $8,500,000 are rendered necessary for increased storage capacity in the old section of the port of Quebec. In asking for this money we are supported not only by individuals, by the people of Quebec, but by the shipping federation. We are supported by persons interested in the grain trade, by persons who are supposed to know something about that business. And these persons are to be found not only in the city of Quebec but throughout Canada. What we are asking for has nothing to do with adding to the facilities for disposing of grain in the elevator at Quebec. I stated in 1925 that the present facilities, so far as the elevator is concerned, could handle 40,000,000 bushels of grain, supposing that the 2,000,000 bushel elevator were used all the time. But we are not asking for any increased facilities for disposing of grain; what we want is greater storage capacity.
Howr much?

Double the present storage
capacity.
What is that?

At present it is 2,000,000
bushels, and we are asking for an additional
2,000,000.

What is the estimated
cost?	.

About $1,900,000 for the
storage capacity. The balance of the money required is to reconstruct and repair the present wharves in order to permit the advantageous use of this increased storage capacity in the old section of the port of Quebec.

Quebec Harbour Commission
We are also asking for a certain amount, which is included in the $8,500,000, to meet certain debentures due the public. The harbour commission of Quebec owes the public over $1,150,000.

Are they guaranteed by
the Dominion?

They were given under the old commission, and we have to meet these debentures maturing presently. All these items are included in the $8,500,000, but what is needed to complete the works undertaken in 1925 and 1926 is the sum of $5,300,000. This will complete the program which has been advocated and supported very strongly by the shipping federation, not only at the request of the people of Quebec but because the members of that federation are convinced that it is absolutely necessary that Quebec be developed more extensively in order to take care of the traffic which should go through that port.
When it is said that we have no justification to offer for this vote, may I ask this question:	What better proof, what more
urgent request could be suggested than the demand of the shipping federation, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways, as well as the request of the very people who are interested in the grain trade? Even if this matter were submitted to a committee, no one could bring forward anything which would add strength to our argument, for the reason that no stronger support could be given that argument than it has already received in writing from these various quarters. What would be the use of bringing these people before a committee to repeat orally what they have already stated in writing? What they stated in writing two years ago, in the representations they made to the government, is much stronger than anything that might be said orally if they were called before a committee. These are the people whose word we are taking in coming before parliament and asking for this money.
It is all very well to say that the port of Quebec has not shown the same prosperity or the same financial development as the port of Vancouver, and that Quebec has not been paying interest. But the same criticism could be made against all other public institutions to which we have advanced money in the past. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member (Mr. Cahan) have said, "Oh, well, the position is different. You have a commission at Quebec, while at St. John, Fort William and Port Arthur there is no commission." Well, this is only an
objection to form and procedure. But what is the real meat of the matter? I submit it is the money which is advanced by the government to any corporation or institution. If we are not getting any return from the port of Quebec we are in no worse position than in respect of moneys we have advanced to other ports or public bodies that have been organized in the country. The ' objection, I say, is a question of form, and I am free to say that I am almost ready to concur in the views expressed by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. It may be that the present system of handling these affairs through a commisison is not the proper one. I have my doubts on the point and I am ready to take the committee into my confidence to the extent of stating that I am considering another scheme of dealing with the business of all our ports in Canada.

ducted that hitherto they have resulted in an annual deficit.
