All the property of the city of Toronto, including Ashbridge's bay and the docks, wharves and land along this waterfront, was turned over to the harbour commissioners of Toronto who have administered it since. There was no provision in the act by which the harbour

Quebec Harbour Commission
commissioners could secure advances from the Dominion government; on the contrary, they have gone to the public for their money and have borrowed it on bond issues which have been endorsed largely by the city of Toronto. Although the interest on these bonds has not been kept up out of the proceeds of the harbour, the deficit has been made up by the corporation of the city of Toronto, and the bonds are in good standing with all payments made to date. The city of Toronto has never come to this parliament for any advance whatever on account of its harbour. It has been suggested by hon. members opposite that because there is an amusement park in the west end of the city called Sunnyside, and another in the. east end called Scarborough, the moneys of the Dominion have gone towards the establishment and maintenance of these parks, but that is a misapprehension; not one dollar has gone for that purpose. These lands have been reclaimed at the expense of the city of Toronto; the parks have been laid out, the buildings erected and the property managed by the harbour commissioners out of the revenues of the harbour chiefly derived from lands turned over by the city, supplemented by the amounts the city of Toronto has been obliged to pay. I should say that for every dollar spent by the Dominion government on navigation five to six dollars of city money have been added to the funds of the harbour commissioners. You might as well talk of charging interest on the money expended in dredging the river channel between Montreal and Quebec as to mention charging interest on the expenditures for navigation purposes at either Port Arthur or Toronto. It is the same thing, and as my leader has said, in every case the appropriation and expenditure of the money placed at the disposal of the harbour commissioners of the port of Toronto for navigation purposes has been under the scrutiny of this parliament.
Perhaps that will settle this point in the minds of hon. members of the house, and I have only a word to add in regard to the proposal now before us. I understood the Minister of Justice to say that out of the amount now asked for, some $5,310,000 is required to complete the work for which this parliament appropriated $5,000,000 only three years ago. The terms of that appropriation were very definite; it was worded as follows:
.... such sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of five million dollars, as may be required to enable the corporation to complete the construction of terminal facilities in the harbour of Quebec, for which the plans, specifications and estimates have been approved by the governor in council before the passing of this act; and to construct. . . .

It does not say to begin the construction, or to construct in part.
.... such additional terminal facilities as may be likewise approved as necessary, further to properly equip the said port.
My understanding of the situation, as outlined" by the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, is that this $5,000,000 improvement has been started, and it has been found impossible to complete the work with the sum voted. Whether it was estimated wrongly at the time or whether it was known that $5,000,000 would not be sufficient I do not know, but it would appear that $5,000,000 is only half enough. The works are in an incomplete state, partly under water; they will be lost if further moneys are not voted, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries asks for $5,310,000 to complete works which it was obviously contemplated would be completed for $5,000,000. We have not been told whether that is the result of a bad estimate; apparently something is wrong with the estimate of $5,000,000 which was presented to this house in 1925. That has not been sufficient for the work, and we are now asked for $5,310,000 more to complete it. As far as I can see that is the situation; in 1925 the harbour commissioners of Quebec contemplated this work, but whether they expected to spend $10,000,000 on the work then in prospect we do not know. If they did it was wrong of them to ask this house for only $5,000,000, saying that that would complete the work, and on the other hand if they miscalculated the cost and now find themselves saddled with a work which will cost over $10,000,000 on which they had expected to spend only $5,000,000, there is something radically wrong with the construction department of the Quebec harbour commission.
The second amount asked for is $2,840,000. I only need refer to the remarks of my hon. friend from Acadia to show that the expenditure of that amount on a storage elevator is not justified by the business which may be expected. We are going to spend over $2,000,000 for further storage; that is an important matter, as the Minister of Railways has said, but you can tell almost to the cent what will be the income from that expenditure. You know the rates for storage, you know the period for which storage will be used, you have the cost of management, and when it is proposed to provide storage facilities for an additional 2,000,000 bushels of grain it is possible to say whether or not you are justified in making that expenditure in view of what you will get in the way of returns. That is not a matter which has to do with the port- of Quebec as far as the

Quebec Harbour Commission
passing through of grain goes. The facilities at that port to-day are acknowledged to be more than are required for all the grain that can reasonably be expected to pass through that port. They will take care of 40,000,000 bushels of grain in the season, and even with the reduced freight rate the volume of grain handled there has only risen to 10,000,000 bushels. So that four times the amount of business actually done in Quebec is already provided for. Surely we do not need to contemplate that feature at all. The only question then remaining as to the $2,980,000 is, will it pay? Is it good business to put up a 2,000,000 bushel storage elevator considering what the returns from that elevator will be? As to the remaining item of $350,000, it is a matter of refunding to which no objection can be made. May I point out to the minister that if this were a going concern which- had been meeting its fixed charges and its operating cost, to say nothing of depreciation, we might have been justified in advancing the sum of $8,500,000 because the returns would be in sight, but in the case of the Quebec harbour we know the interest on the loans is in arrears, and we know moreover from the auditors' report that there is no prospect of ever collecting that interest. Therefore you are going into a proposition in which the interest and fixed charges, to say nothing of other items, cannot be met. The right policy to pursue is to follow the course which has been suggested by my leader to scrutinize carefully every item and consider whether the expenditure is justified, not only from the point of view of dollars and cents but from the point of view of making Quebec a great national harbour and maintaining it as such.
Once more, may I say that I regret exceedingly the tone that was taken by the Minister of Justice in his remarks this afternoon, remarks which to some extent reflected the feelings of others. Personally I should like to see the port of Quebec developed, or any other port on the east or west coast developed, if it is going to add to the general prosperity of Canada. It is a small thing to accuse any hon. member, even by implication, of being influenced in his attitude by local attachment. That is nonsense in the case of myself, and I know that in saying that I can speak for others both to the right and left of me. We desire to look at this as a national matter. The fact that we are dealing with the port of Quebec-and we are all proud of that city and its historic associations-does not enter
into the matter at all, nor the fact that it is not Toronto; and if the Minister of Justice, and one or two others, suggest that we are influenced in our attitude by local prejudice, they are following a course which is entirely wrong.

I do not see why this port should not have its votes in the estimates, and not by resolution. The trouble in the administration of these ports is that politics has been rampant in them. The government in my opinion are spending money like water. Money has been spent on some ports and canals in this country which never should have been spent; money that should have been spent has not been spent, and in many cases practically every dollar of that expenditure has been wasted. There has been no well conceived general plan of development. We have been creating ports on the great lakes where the expenditure has been used for political purposes. The same can be said of some of the canals. I know a canal where it was customary to start work a month before every election but after the election was over that expenditure was discontinued. There are instances of this kind in almost every province in the Dominion. The port of Montreal is in politics to-day. The elevator business is also in politics. The grain trade is in politics. The railways, also the canals, are in politics. Canada is more cursed with partyism than any other country in the world. We can solve no economic problems at all in this parliament, all such questions are referred to the courts or to a commission. The port of Quebec is a great port with a history dating back over three hundred years but it has never had a chance; the politicians have killed it. The Liberal party which launched the Grand Trunk Pacific is responsible for all the railway ills of this country to-day as well as for all the evils that have grown up in connection with our ports and grain trade. I know of no agencies where politics have been used to a greater extent than in connection with the port of Quebec, the administration of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and the ad-ministiation of the national railways under the present chairman. The port of Quebec will never have a chance against the port of Montreal until its administration is freed from politics. It used to be said that New York and Boston were the great ports of the Atlantic seaboard of the United States; now there are nine or ten fine ports along that sea coast from Boston to Savannah. Every one of these ports is prospering and the ships which enter and leave them are gather-

Quebec Harbour Commission
ing business from the seven seas. Have we seen any like development in the case of our ports? The ills the maritime provinces are suffering from to-day are largely due to politics, and politics prevailed to a very great extent in the administration of the Intercolonial railway. The Quebec bridge was built and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway constructed to help Quebec and the grain trade.
The great port of Vancouver handled 53,000,000 bushels through one elevator which I saw when I was there last year and which has a capacity of only 1,250,000 to 1,500,000 bushels. The opening of the Panama canal has revolutionized matters of transportation on the North American continent and particularly in regard to the transportation of grain from the prairie provinces. You will never settle this grain problem while it is in politics. The elevator question is in polities; the port of Quebec is in politics, and as regards the grain policy of this country you will never get any more grain passing through the city of Quebec until you change your elevator and grain policy. We had a royal commission appointed in 1924 to investigate this question. What did they recommend? They recommended that an embargo be placed upon hard wheat going to the United States, as will be found at page 145 of their report. It was a hard struggle to get this commission appointed; I was in the house at the time, and I made some comments and charges in regard to bootlegging of Canadian grain and the elevators at Buffalo and New York. The government said that this was not so; but when the evidence was taken, it was proved that it was so; that bootlegging in grain was taking place at Buffalo and New York, United States wheat being mixed with Canadian and the flour shipped overseas as number one to the detriment of Canada.
The minister is not handling this question in the proper manner, although I do not wish to blame the present minister entirely. He could not find a five dollar bill for life saving stations in the upper great lakes to protect the lives of our brave sailors who are endeavouring to advance the grain from the prairie provinces to the seaports. Last month an American life saving tug from Ashtabula arrd Erie, Pennsylvania, had to come up and take some men off a tug caught in the ice on lake Erie. What did the Ontario government do? They sent a wire to Hon. Mr. Martin, the Minister of Agriculture congratulating him on his forethought in getting a United States tug to save a few Canadian sailors on lake Erie.

What did the Minister of Marine and Fisheries do last session with regard to grain? He is talking about getting more grain to Quebec. He had the coastal laws suspended on the Great Lakes, with the result that our boats are lying up at the docks and all the grain is going to fill American hulls. Last summer I saw in the Detroit river, United States ships carrying our grain down to Buffalo, where during the past few years they have erected twenty-eight elevators. What does the commissioner of industries of Buffalo say about this matter? One of the main things in his report is that he takes pride in the fact that they have been able to get Canada's hard wheat to fill up twenty-eight elevators at Buffalo where they can bootleg our grain and mill it into flour for export. Every Canadian would rejoice to see those twenty-eight elevators erected in Quebec, Montreal, and other places along the gulf of St. Lawrence, where they would be if this country had a proper grain policy, and a proper water-borne traffic through Canadian ports overseas.
After all is said and done, the discussion initiated by hon. members on this side of the house will do a great deal of good if it can persuade the government that we have had enough politics in regard to this matter. The Hon. Mr. Hoover has spoken, in a report to congress and to the Interstate Commerce Commission about this particular problem, and in his report he refers to the great ports in his own country on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts. He says that a definite, well-worked out scheme, like those which New York, Boston and Baltimore have, should be adopted and that before votes of money occur or are gone ahead -with, competent engineers should be employed to investigate the whole question from engineering, financial, navigation, and economic standpoints. It must not be forgotten while this vote for Quebec harbour is under discussion, that as regards the export of our grain, the overseas market with regard to grain has all been changed. Argentina and Russia are back in the market and many of the Balkan states and others are back to-day competing with our grain growers for the overseas markets of the world. The result is that the grain situation in the old world has been changed and we have been sitting here spending millions of dollars on some of our ports without any results as to routing Canadian grain in mass through our gulf and coast ports.
The port of Quebec could, in my opinion, be made a great port if we had a well-worked out economic plan. Last year I visited it for

Quebec Harbour Commission
the first time in twenty years; it is suffering from congestion owing to lack of modern facilities for handling the freight traffic. It will never be a port except for five and a half months in the year, and it will be a grain port only if it has the support of an allCanadian rail route and waterborne traffic route for grain and an adequate and economic storage capacity. It will be a good storage place for grain forwarded there late in the year and held in the elevator for spring shipment overseas. I understand that the capacity of the Quebec elevator is only 2,000,000 bushels and that last year they handled out of that port only about nine or ten million bushels, whereas at Vancouver with an elevator with a capacity of 1,500,000 'bushels they were able to handle 53,000,000 bushels.
Reference has been made to other ports, and there has been a very wide discussion of the policy of this country in general in regard to national ports and ports on the great lakes. There are a few ports like Montreal and Vancouver which pay the interest on their indebtedness. The quantity of grain shipped through the port of Montreal during the last few years is as follows:
Year	Bushels
1921		 138,000,000
1922		 135,000,000
1923		 120,000,000
1924		 165,000,000
1925		 166,000,000
1926		 135,000,000
1927		 185,000,000
Let us not forget that last year there landed in the port of Montreal 80,000,000 bushels of grain from the United States. We are pursuing a very foolish policy on the great lakes in regard to grain. We have amended the coastal laws with the result that our own Canadian boats are tied up at the docks and our United States competitors are getting all this grain. Is that a proper policy for the people of this country? No, we must change our whole grain policy and adopt the recommendation of the commission by imposing an embargo and utilizing all-Canadian routes to get our grain through to the seaboard in Canadian hulls.
The government has been spending money like water. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier announced his Grand Trunk Pacific scheme away back in 1896, it took $36,000,000 to run and maintain the country, whereas to-day it is taking $400,000,000 a year to run the country. The province of Ontario used to get along with an expenditure of $6,500,000, but to-day it alone is spending $57,000,000 a year, or $21,000,000 more than it cost to run the whole country in 1897.
Some reference was made by hon. gentleman opposite to the port from which I came. Let me tell the Progressive members of this house that the port of Toronto has never got the loan of a copper from the government of Canada. Since confederation only ten millions have been spent by the government on Toronto harbour. The taxpayers of Toronto have themselves spent $30,000,000 on harbour improvements. Any money the government spends it handles itself free from the city or harbour board. From 1867 to 1912 only $2,000,000 were spent by the government. In 1912 the port was reorganized, and the harbour board has jurisdiction only over city property in the harbour. The government never built a dock or a wharf in Toronto, and Toronto harbour right down to the present time never got a five cent piece by way of loan from the government. There are five commissioners under the new scheme, three appointed by the city council and two by the government, and the two commissioners appointed by the government are on the city board spending city money. The government spends its own money and it has built a seawall, a turning basin in Ashbridge's bay and dredged the entrances. The late Lieutenant Governor Clarke, Mr. Smith and I were commissioners, and we had a non-political board for twenty years, until 1925. It was the present government's two delegates that caused all the recent trouble; the government appointed two politicians or ward-heelers, and they tried to work a city board on a Liberal basis with the taxpayers' money, mind you, not the government's. I was a commissioner without a cent of remuneration, for twenty years. I was appointed by the city council and I worked all that time with my colleagues. We never had any politics on the board till 1925. A gentleman by the name of MacKendrick, appointed by the city in 1924, joined the two Liberals and while he was a commissioner, he tried to buy a large property at a cut rate for his company on Fleet stret. I objected to this as improper, and an illegal government inquiry was started over a purely city board, spending only city money and not a cent of government money, by a person who, while acting, had, according to the harbour board's own solicitor, Mr. A. C. McMaster, K.C., and the government's own legal officers, no powers, and acted only voluntarily. Well, they had a year's inquiry over nothing, with nice, fat fees for the judge, although, while sitting he was neither judge nor commissioner, and a number of lawyers got fat fees as was the case in the customs inquiry. They spent $75,000 of the taxpayers' money,

Quebec Harbour Commission
found not a cent misspent or a thing wrong, if you please, on this investigation; they did not get anybody, nor did they find out anything. The only body they got was the taxpayer. Mr. Home Smith and Lieutenant-Governor Clarke served for many years without fee or reward. I myself served for twenty years on the harbour board, and got nothing for it; all we got was abuse. I spent thousands of dollars of my own money also in the work. We were a non-political board until two disturbers appeared with political minds. While I was chairman of the harbour board I settled the viaduct case long standing, opened up Fleet street, and made rapid strides. I resigned my seat voluntarily. After this farce of an inquiry the city council unanimously reappointed me, but I got sick of the work and the abuse and gave up this end of my work after twenty years full service.
If you want to make a success of the port of Quebec or any other port you must eliminate politics; in other words, as Mr. Hoover says, you must have a non-political administration of the board. The port must be administered from an economic standpoint. If the port of Quebec had been given any chance at all, it would have been a great port to-day, but the money that has been voted for the port of Quebec has not been spent to the best advantage and the same is true to a certain extent of Montreal. They take on a large staff in Montreal, I am told just before election time, and then turn them off after the election. The port is in politics. I think every Canadian is proud of the port of Montreal. I am a warm supporter of Montreal, and I believe that it will grow from strength to strength as a port if the commissioners are let alone.
The government have now had considerable experience in connecttion with these various harbours, which should be an example to them, and let us make a fresh start with Halifax and St. John by administering these new ports from the commercial aspect. We can still do something with Quebec, but I do not believe in giving $8,500,000 to the port of Quebec at the present time. I was in the house in 1925 when Mr. Caldwell and the present member for Macleod, in reply to questions, were informed by the minister that the $5,000,000 that was being voted at that time for the port of Quebec would be sufficient to complete the whole five years' program. Only three years have passed since then, and here is the harbour commission back again asking for $8,500,000 more. It will take a lot of money to provide the necessary extensions for handling the grain, but even 
when that work is finished, I doubt if any more grain will go to the port, because the Canadian National Railways are not trying to help the port of Quebec.
Those of us on this side of the house, Mr. Chairman, would like to see the port of Quebec dealt with fairly and justly and equitably, the same as any other port. We must not forget that these ports are a connecting link in a well organized transportation system, but we have not a properly connected transportation system in this country because our transportation system is mixed up in politics. The ports are also in politics, and you will never get them out of politics until public opinion drives them out.
The province of Ontario pays forty-nine per cent of the postal receipts of this Dominion. The city of Toronto contributes $62,000,000 in customs duties, and well on to $7,000,000 in postal receipts, and we have never got a cent from the government during the last four sessions except a few dollars for revolving doors for the post office, and when that item is reached I am going to move to strike it out.

What about the terminals
costing $1,500,000 last year?

What about terminals?
Let me tell the minister about the terminals. He is a new minister here, and he seems to think he knows something about the Toronto terminals, but I think he knows more about elections and the ballot boxes in New Brunswick.

The people know how to
handle the ballots.
Mr. CHURCH; I do not want to be unfair to the minister because he supported my newspaper bill to make public the ownership of newspapers, and to let everyone know who Mr. Honourable-in-Trust is in connection with some of these newspapers. The city of Toronto itself spent $30,000,000 on its own property-the harbour.
Mr. VENIOT; I was referring to the postal terminals, not the railway terminals.

The government spent
some money on the postal terminals, but they get a revenue of yearly $7,000,000 out of the Toronto post office. The minister has a patronage list in the post office department, and you have to pay a dollar to join the Liberal ward association before you can get a temporary job. Even a returned soldier in Christie street hospital, if he wants a job at the post office for five or six days at Christmas time, has to pay a dollar and join

Quebec Harbour Commission
the ward association. There is no city in Canada that is paying the peak of taxation like Toronto is. We have spent $30,000,000 of our own money on our harbour, and if it had not been for the harbour improvements and breakwater at Sunnyside the right of way of the Canadian National railway would have been washed out. Eight millions were spent (1914-1924) by the government on the harbour. About $2,500,000 of this was spent on a breakwater to protect the right of way of the Canadian National railway, and a contract as to the harbour in 1912 was made with the city of Toronto and the federal government, and this government is trying to back out of it. The city of Toronto has spent over $10,000,000 on the viaduct agreement on the water front and thirty millions on its harbour besides. We seek no favours from the government; we would not get any anyway, and we do not ask for them, no matter what government is in office.
So far as the port of Quebec is concerned, I agree with the leader of the opposition that this vote ought to be cut down, and an interim grant of $1,000,000 or $1,500,000 made, this year; and a proper survey should be made of the business of the port and its finances and terminals. The grain law of Canada should be revolutionized in the interest of Canadian ports, and the coasting laws should be re-established. There should be a showdown with the Canadian National Railways to further help the ports of Montreal and Quebec. There should be non-political administration of the port of Quebec and all the other ports. The port of Vancouver has been ruined through the dismissal of one of the ablest traffic superintendents on the North American continent, as the hon. member for Vancouver said in the house last night. There should be a non-political administration of these ports, a proper survey made of the business of the port, and expenditure made on business principles; for at present money is being spent like water on ports and harbours. Money is being spent on ports where there is not a ship, and when the pork barrel is opened up, they sometimes vote money for harbours where there is not even a row boat. I do not say that that is true of the port of Quebec. I believe that Quebec never had a fair show. Take politics out of the administration of the port and have a proper survey made by reliable engineers, not the kind of a survey that was made in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, which it was estimated would cost only a few million dollars instead of one hundred millions. We should get a proper survey of Quebec harbour and an up-to-date plan even if we have to
go to Great Britain for engineers. Go and get them, and have a survey and permanent plan of development made of the port of Quebec. I venture to think that every good Canadian, when this is done, will rejoice to see the great port of Quebec go ahead by leaps and bounds and get a fair share of the gain and other traffic from the interior of Canada. What I have said of the port of Quebec will apply also to the ports of St. John and Halifax when organized.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the citizens of Quebec and hon. members who are interested in the port must feel gratified at the almost unanimous desire expressed on both sides of the house to see the port of Quebec improved to accommodate the great ocean traffic now developing there. But the trouble is we have been debating this question now for almost two days without making any progress, and our friends who are interested in the port may begin to question the sincerity of those who speak so well of Quebec. My hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Church) has told us about the great port of Toronto, and has emphasized the point that during the period when he was on the harbour board it was a non-political organization. I think I shall be well within the mark when I say that the board of harbour commissioners of Quebec is justly as non-political as my hon. friend's board.
I agree with much that has been said tonight as to our having spent a lot of money on our ports for which the country has not received the value that it should have received, and the records of the public accounts wrill confirm this. I observe, for instance, that we have spent some $21,000,000 on the port of St. John. Well, mo one will say that that is a better port than Quebec. We have spent on the lake port of Toronto-I am not finding any fault; I am simply placing the facts before the committee-through the Public Works Department between ten and eleven million dollars. My hon. friend from Toronto Northwest says that the port never got a copper from the Dominion, but apparently he has not looked at the public accounts.
He said in the nature of advances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite right; we paid out the money and did not expect to get it. back.
It was not a loan, it was contributed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the fact remains we spent $10,000,000 on the port of Toronto.

There is no question of that

Quebec Harbour Commission

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No one will argue that the port of Quebec, where the ocean traffic of the world comes, is not entitled to equal consideration. No one will challenge the point raised 'by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that wherever public moneys are paid out there should be a careful audit. But after all that is exactly the position we are in to-day.
May I point out to the minister that the 810,000,000 was spent by the Public Works department; the city of Toronto had no control over it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly; 'but the money was paid out of the exchequer. We have the right, and we exercise it, to insist on the most careful scrutiny wherever public money is expended. Now the port of Quebec asks for an advance of sufficient money to take care of its harbour plans for the next five years. Everyone will agree that to do such work economically and efficiently we must be able to lay out a program extending over a period of years. No advance is made until a report is received from the engineers indicating the progress of the work. I believe there is a superintendent of harbours who checks up the work of the port engineer. That report is sent to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, wher;e it is carefully checked, and then the accounts are senit to the Department of Finance before the advance is made.
Are advances made to the harbour commission of Quebec on monthly applications from the commission to the minister, giving the amount of construction work to be done and detailed statements?

The procedure followed at Quebec is the same as that followed at Montreal. The work is executed, a report is made by the commission to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, that report is checked by us, and when we are satisfied we ask the Department of Finance to advance the money.
On monthly applications?
No.
That is the procedure followed in the case of Montreal.
Not necessarily.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then these advances are made. Bear in mind, the accounts are carefully audited. We insist on an additional audit wherever these expenditures are made. We have a perfect right, for example, to check the expenditures made in the port of Halifax.

I have not heard any person say yet that the money spent there was spent bo the best advantage. It is quite true, as hon. gentlemen say, that we have wasted money. But we are all aware that government expenditure is never made as cheaply as private expenditure.

Will the minister permit a question before he leaves that point? He is dealing with the system of audit. Will he kindly explain these statements in the report of the board of audit that checked the port of Quebec's accounts?
Examination of the published reports clearly shows the expenses to have increased steadily and out of proportion to the earnings during the three years.
And:
The accounts examined by us provided no explanation for these variations, due largely to the suspension some years ago of cost accounts.
Now I put this question to the minister, having some knowledge of the meaning of this language: upon receiving a report of this character from a board of auditors appointed for the purpose of examining these accounts, does he think it a wise policy to make any' further advances before some adequate explanation is forthcoming of what I would call a dereliction of duty on the part of the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was just coming to that. I imagine that when I send out the audit board, as I intend to, to audit other ports we may have similar reports to this.

These insinuations might as well ibe cleared up at once. I ask the minister now to instruct the board of audit, to check carefully the expenditures at the port of Vancouver-the papers in connection with which I called for and they were laid on the table- because I think some of those expenditures were recklessly, extravagantly, improvidently and wrongfully made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to the contract for the Ballantyne pier?
No, I am not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought not. I was proceeding to say that the government has the right to go in. It was for that very purpose that the audit board was created under the act assented to on June 27, 1925. Here are the powers of the audit board covering this point:
It shall be the duty of the board to act in an advisory capacity to the treasury board and

Quebec Harbour Commission
under its direction to inquire into and report with regard to any matters entrusted to it by the treasury board including the following:
(a)	the sufficiency of the methods of accounting and of the procedure in other respects employed in the conduct of the public business of Canada or of any department or detail thereof;
(b)	the economies which may be effected in any of the public services or in the conduct of the public business;
(c)	the financial affairs of the Canadian National Railway Company and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, and any other undertaking owned or carried on by the government of Canada;
(d)	-
-and I direct my hon. friend's attention to this:
(d)	the financial affairs of any commission or other public body the operations of which are carried on by appropriations from the treasury of Canada, or which are aided by grants or loans from the said treasury.
It is under that that we have the board look into the accounts. The question asked by my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) is a very proper one, but the chairman of the audit board has informed me that he has had a talk with the commission and they recognize that their system of accounts might very well be changed so as to afford more information. And the system of accounts will be changed. But there is no report that the contracts were irregular or that there were any irregular expenditures. Now I come back to this point: To carry on the work successfully and economically they must be able to lay out a program for more than one year, and it is not unreasonable to give them a sufficient sum to cover a period of five years. They say that this amount is * required for a five year program, and I can assure my hon. friends that under the Audit Act we have full powers to go and audit their accounts. And it is our intention to do so in respect to that port as well as in respect to others in Canada.

I asked a question of the minister and 'he was kind enough to answer. I asked the question after a hasty glance over the act passed last year covering the loan made to the Montreal harbour commission. I found that in connection with that commission a certain course was taken to safeguard the interests of Canada in doing business with the port of Montreal. I found in the first place that before the money was granted the plans had to be approved by the governor in council. That seemed to be wise and businesslike. Monthly statements were also required to be presented by the harbour commission to the minister in connection with applications for loans on account of construction work being performed. A
detailed statement of expenditures in connection therewith was submitted. That also struck me as a very wise provision inasmuch as it kept the minister constantly in touch with what was going on. In view of these provisions in connection with the Montreal harbour commission I asked the minister a question in regard to the present resolution and I understood him to say the same course was not being followed in relation to advances to the harbour commission of Quebec. I notice that there was a further safeguard in the case of the Montreal harbour commission, in that the corporation deposited with the Minister of Finance debentures equal in value to the loan asked for. That, too, was good business. It is a fact that in 1925 the sum of $5,000,000 was advanced to the Quebec harbour commission and we were told at that time that this sum would be sufficient to complete certain works. It is now apparent that it will not be adequate to complete the works which it was said it would take care of, and we are now asked for further millions to supplement that grant. The minister has said that certain statements are presented-he has not told us at what intervals

to his department in regard to these expenditures. One would expect such statements to be submitted. But why not follow the same course in dealing with the harbour commission of Quebec as was adopted in connection with the harbour commission of Montreal? Why not require monthly statements presented to the minister, giving a detailed account of construction work undertaken and of the moneys expended thereon? That seems to be a reasonable course, and I cannot help thinking that if the same method had been followed in the case of the Quebec port the government would have been more in touch with what has been going on, and the financial condition of the port would not be as bad as it is at the present time.

When I replied to my hon. friend from Frontenac a few minutes ago I spoke from memory in regard to advances made in the past. I notice that in the bill which will be introduced following the resolution there is a clause providing for monthly applications and monthly statements from the commission before they can get any money. So that the clause in the Montreal act to which my hon. friend has referred-I do not know whether it is in the Quebec act of 1925 -will be found in the bill which we propose to introduce on the basis of this resolution.

That was
wise. Can the minister inform the committee
219S

Quebec Harbour Commission
just how frequently these statements have been presented in the past covering the $5,000,000 advanced in 1925? Apparently they have not been presented monthly.

Offhand I cannot say, but
I shall be in a position to give this information definitely when we reach the committee stage on the bill. As regards my hon. friend's observation with reference to the adequacy of the 85,000,000, I may say that this amount is sufficient to meet the requirements we had in view in 1925. The money has not all been spent, and the vote for which we are now asking is for the purpose of adding to the facilities which were provided for through the advance made in 1925.

How much
of the $5,000,000 voted in 1925 has been spent?

As I understand it, the
harbour commission now owe $750,000 to the banks, presumably for current obligations. We are voting $8,500,000 for additional facilities. The minister has stated that the port has claims against the government amounting to something over $7,000,000. No doubt the government is considering that $7,000,000 odd in addition to the $8,500,000. If that sum were paid over this year or next year, as an obligation which we owe to the board, would the board have the power to add still further facilities or would they be obliged to use this money in paying interest on the loans advanced?

The claims of the commissioners are set up against the government's claim for interest. The government is claiming $8,000,000 or arrears in interest on moneys which have been advanced to the Quebec harbour commission. The commissioners say, "Well, you claim that interest, but we have a claim against the government for taking care of the immigrants and for other services. Our claim amounts to almost $7,000,000. and we would like to set that off against the claim of the government for interest on the loans which have been made to us." They are not asking for payment but simply that their claim be accepted to apply against the amount of interest claimed by the government.

Then we are in the position of lending them $8,500,000 and allowing the interest to be offset by claims against the government; in other words we not only lend them money but pay the interest as well.

That is the claim of the
commissioners, but as yet the government have not decided to accept it.

At this point I should
like to ask the minister as to the attitude of the government in regard to these claims. How long have they been in existence, and what is the government going to do about them?

These claims have been in existence for a long period of years, and I am free to say that the accounts sent in by the commissioners have not been accepted by the various departments to which they were sent. There is no doubt that the commissioners are entitled to something for having taken care of the immigrants and so on; they are entitled to some compensation, but up to the present that claim has not been accepted by the departments concerned.

Why not charge it up to the
Department of Immigration?
It is charged to that department, but the various ministers of immigration have refused to accept it.
The minister has just admitted that there is some justice in the claims made by the harbour commissioners against the various departments. When did he arrive at that conclusion?

I have been of that opinion always, but I cannot force my views or con. victions upon my colleagues. I am convinced that the commissioners should receive something, if not the whole amount; they should receive a certain compensation, but up to the present time the successive ministers of immigration have refused to accept my views.

Does not the minister
think that before any further loans are made to the harbour commission the question of these claims should be settled? Is not this a good time to settle them?

I cannot see any relation
between the two matters. The claim of the government is for interest from the harbour commission, and that is quite different from the advance for which we are asking at present. If these accounts are accepted from the harbour commissioners, the amount will be set off against the claim of the government for the unpaid interest.

What difference would it
make in the long run?

Quebec Harbour Commission

It is simply a matter of
bookkeeping, but the position of the harbour commissioners will be more clearly presented because a large proportion of their indebtedness for interest will disappear if their claims are entertained.
Cannot the cabinet as a whole settle that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The cabinet as a whole did settle the question of the remission of a considerable amount of money to the Soldier Settlement Board, and the remission of advances for seed grain.

Those matters have no relation to the subject under discussion, but with respect to the other question, in my judgment the minister cannot say it has no relation to the matter with which we are now dealing. The relation I see is this:	Just so
long as the claims of the harbour commission remain against the government, that provides them an excuse to refuse to pay interest, which means that the harbour will not be operated as efficiently as should be the case. Now I should like to ask the minister if he could give me the information I asked for before six o'clock. I notice that the Minister of Immigration is smiling; probably he would not be quite so joyous if a part of his appropriation were taken to pay some of these just claims. Can the Minister of Marine and Fisheries give the committee any information as to the expenditures which have been made out of the 85,000,000 loan since 1925? How much has been actually spent in dredging, providing new wharves and so on, and what is the condition of the work at present?

I am not in a position to give a detailed statement of the expenditures which have been made, but as I said a moment ago-and that was only a repetition of what I have said several times before-out of the $5,000,000 voted in 1925 approximately $3,000,000 has been- expended in dredging and in the construction of the cribs which have been filled with stone and sunk into the river. The work remaining is the concrete work upon those cribs, and the balance of the money to which the commissioners are entitled will complete the cement work which was provided for in 1925. The $5,300,000 in addition for which we are now asking is to extend that part of the work which is covered by the $5,000,000 voted in 1925, of which nearly $3 000,000 has been expended already. There remains the concrete work and the construction of certain sheds and roadways upon these cribs.

I understand that the minister's reply is to the effect that in so far as the vote of 1925 is concerned, the work contemplated under that vote is only partly completed, but that sufficient funds still remain to complete the work as contemplated at that time. Further, I understand that the new vote which we are discussing to-night is to provide for an extension of that work?
Yes.

I am glad to have that information; we have been trying to get it ever since this resolution was introduced. Now I want to ask the minister whether in view of the contemplated new work, which will eventually cost $8,500.000-
It w'ill cost $5,000,000.
That is right, $5,310,000. In view of that, will the minister give us some information as to the tonnage into and out of the port, which will warrant this contemplated construction?

The committee will understand that it is very difficult to say what tonnage will pass through the port of Quebec in the years to come. However, for the information of my hon. friend I might say that in 1926 about. 900 ocean steamers went into and out of the port of Quebec, and the total tonnage was 6,408,059. In 1927, although the new terminals constructed out of the $5,000,000 voted in 1925 were not in use, the tonnage was 6.820,375, so there was an increase of over 400.000 tons without taking into consideration the new facilities.

How many steamers
were there that year?

The total would be about
900, but I am not sure as to the exact number. If the reduction in rates on the Transcontinental will have the effect of causing a greater volume of grain to flow through the port of Quebec we may reasonably expect a greater tonnage. We have to recognize that ocean vessels are becoming larger and larger and that each year the tonnage will be greater. As I said at the opening of this discussion the shipping interests are behind these improvements and they say:	In view of the
developments and the needs of the port, we support heartily the program of the harbour commission. But my hon. friend will clearly understand that I cannot give any definite figure as to the prospective increase in tonnage.

Quebec Harbour Commission

Would it not be reasonable to suppose that when the present works are completed, that is to say the works undertaken under the $5,000,000 vote of 1925, they will take care of all the requirements in increased tonnage for some years to come?
Mr, CARDIN:	The representations which
were made to the commission and to the government were in support of the program we are contemplating at the present time, including the additional work. The representations of the shipping federation and of the grain people not only supported the improvements decided upon in 1925 but requested new undertakings. They feel that an expenditure which will run to about $10,000,000 should be made to equip properly the port of Quebec and give it the facilities which they think are absolutely necessary. That is the representation which has been made to us.

Without disturbing the minister's argument further, will the sinking of the sixteen cribs, and the placing of the superstructure upon them, require more than the original $5,000,000 before this work is available for use?
No.

Then the remainder of the
$5,310,000 is to produce more cribs, an entirely new proposal?
Yes.

The minister this afternoon gave us some information with regard to the number of berths available in the harbour of Quebec. I notice that he stated a berth was rented to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and another to a second shipping company. Could he give the committee any information as to the rentals paid by the two. companies in question for the private use of these berths?

No, I cannot give the rentals at the present moment. I have certain information here but it is incomplete. The Robert Reford Company, for example, is sending a cheque for $4,000. My notes are not sufficiently complete to permit me to give exact information.
Will the minister secure that information before the bill comes before the committee?
Yes, certainly.

I think it is advisable
for us to know whether or not these rentals are profitable.

I shall be quite ready to
supply the information.

Will the minister have the
plans showing the work contemplated under the $5,000,000 vote in 1925 and the plans of the work contemplated under the present vote?
Certainly.

I should like to draw the minister's attention to claims made upon the Dominion government by the harbour commission of Quebec. There are two items in particular that interest me. One is a claim against the Department of the Interior for $351,437 plus interest of $382,361, and the other a claim against the Department of Immigration for $2,613,716 with accumulated interest of $3,029,070. In each of these claims the interest is a good deal larger than the principal.
Yes.

I should like to point out that at 5 per cent simple interest these amounts must have been running for over 20 years. What rate has been charged on these outstanding accounts? Is it simple or compound interest?

In answer to my hon. friend I want to point out, in order that the matter may be well understood, that the present commission came into existence in 1913, and we have to make a distinction between the loans made since 1913 and whatever advances may have been made previous to that year. The total advances made by the government to the present commission amount to 13i millions. Now the advances made by the government of Canada for the harbour of Quebec from prior to 1867 till 1913-and the harbour was administered by several bodies during that time-amounted to only $4,125,000. Great emphasis has been laid in the present discussion by several gentlemen opposite on the claim that .the harbour board was bankrupt. The leader of the opposition ended his remarks by saying that the board was insolvent and practically in the same position as a commercial corporation in the hands of a receiver. In order to reach that conclusion they charged up against the harbour board an amount of $9,103,899.34 but the present commission should be responsible only for the interest on the advances made since the inception of the commission.
Not if they took over the liabilities of the old board.

I will come to that in a minute. I wish to give these figures: Ad-

Quebec Harbour Commission
vances previous to 1913 by way of accrued interest charged up to the commission, $6,022,565.38; interest on advances made since 1913, $3,081,433.96. But on the $5,000,000 voted by parliament in 1925, or at least on that part of the $5,000,000 which was really advanced, the interest was deducted by the government before the money was paid.
How much was deducted?
Five per cent.
For how many years?

Since 1925. On the advances made under the legislation passed in 1925, the commission does not owe one cent of interest to the government because the Minister of Finance retained it, and this is done in all such cases wherever construction is going on.
It is provided for in this legislation.

Yes. I should like the
members of the committee, in order that they may understand the situation, to bear in mind first that certain moneys were advanced before 1913 when the present harbour commission system did not exist; that the first large advance made to the Quebec harbour with a view of developing Quebec and making it a national port was made in 1913 under the Borden government; that war broke out, and that then the commission had practically to place the harbour in the hands of the government for war purposes. Naturally there was no idea at that time of administering the harbour from the standpoint of making profits and revenues and paying interest. The whole harbour was placed at the disposal of this country, but nevertheless the Minister of Finance every month and every year charged up interest against the port of Quebec.
During the war?

That is something that
must be borne in mind when the general situation of Quebec is under consideration, and it is going too far for any member to say that -the port of Quebec should be considered as bankrupt. The whole harbour facilities were placed in the hands of the Dominion government during the period of the war.
And for two years afterwards.

And for some time afterwards. As everybody knows, many soldiers came back through the port of Quebec, but that peculiar situation was never considered
by the Department of Finance. That is number two. Supposing the same system were adopted for the other harbours in the Dominion, what would be the situation? Last year we incorporated a harbour commission for the city of Halifax. What attitude would hon. members for Halifax or the people of that city have taken if the government had told them: We are incorporating a harbour commission, but before you start developing or looking after the shipping facilities of your harbour, we will charge up to you $19,000,000 which have been already advanced-not only the capital but the interest from the very moment one cent was advanced from the Dominion treasury. Would any hon. member say that that was fair? Nevertheless that is the attitude taken in regard to Quebec harbour. We are not bankrupt if we are treated in the same way as other sections olf Canada have been treated, and the rules which obtain in regard to othtft harbours of this country should obtain in regard to Quebec.
Let me take for instance the harbour of Toronto. I may say to the hon. members for Toronto that I was in their beautiful city last week; I admire its development and the harbour improvements and works; I do not begrudge a cent they received. But would their harbour commission be in a position to make the report which was mentioned by the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) if they had to pay interest on the S10,000,000 which were expended by the Department of Public Works on harbour improvements in Toronto?
I-t is not the same thing. Why should it be?

The interest should be
charged up if Quebec should be charged up with interest. The situation is the same.
Surely the situation is not the same. These are navigation works. You might as well charge up the cost of dredging the river channel opposite Quebec.
Legally my hon. friend is perfectly right.
Practically I am right.

Legally he is perfectly
right, but I am not talking strict law; I am talking equity.
I am not talking law.

I am asking for Quebec fair treatment from this house. I am not quibbling as to the interpretation of statutes; I know there is a difference between a loan and a gift; but if $10,000,000 was given to the

Quebec Harbour Commission
harbour of Toronto, I congratulate my hon. friends on having received that money. I am pleased that they received it. But when the harbour of Quebec comes before parliament asking that we be given the means to improve our harbour facilities, I ask my hon. friends to discard petty and mean considerations and to look at the matter as we should look at it.
Will the minister allow me?

If last year we told Halifax that they would have to assume liability for the $19,000,000 which were expended in that city prior to last year, not only the capital, but the interest, that commission would not be able to work. Supposing when the resolution concerning Halifax is brought before the house, the Quebec members get up and say: Before half a million dollars are advanced, you will have to show that $19,000,000 have been looked after and that eve^y cent of interest has been paid! Supposing we did the same thing concerning St. John, New Brunswick!
You would get killed.

That only goes to show that this matter is not one of dollars and cents and a small matter as to whether interest was paid or not. It is a larger and much wider matter than that. It is a question of finding out if the Dominion government as such and the federal parliament as such wish to develop Canadian trade through Canadian ports or want Canadian trade to go through United States ports. That is the whole question. Hon. members who sit in the corner have shown sympathy.
Be very careful about that.

I think it is a very favoured comer. It has shown some sympathy for the harbour of Quebec. My hon. friends have said, and rightly so, that parliament should be given information. That demand is quite legitimate, and I am quite sure that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries who has charge of this legislation will be pleased to give to the house all necessary information. There is nothing to hide in this matter.
Again I repeat, this is a national question, not one simply of local concern, and we from Quebec ask all our colleagues, whether they belong to the Conservative party or to the Progressive party, to consider this as a national question. In the harbour of Quebec you have, so to speak, the whole question of our national future summed up. When a newcomer enters Canada seeking his fortune,

having confidence in the greatness of our country, where does he land? He lands at Quebec. Where does he go?
To the United States.

He goes to the western provinces. My hon. friend on the other side says that he goes to the United States. He knows better. These newcomers go to the western provinces. My hon. friend forgets that Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta have been built up by these newcomers, and that Canada does not end at the borders of Ontario but stretches farther west. These western provinces produce wheat, and that wheat has to be shipped to some market. Are we going to spend millions to encourage immigration to come to this country in order to develop the natural resources of our western provinces, and then when it comes to marketing the goods these newcomers produce, so that the advantages of our immigration may be realized, refuse to spend the necessary money on our harbours and provide the necessary shipping facilities? I do not think this parliament will hesitate.
It is most unfair, I repeat, to speak of the harbour of Quebec as if it were a corporation which should be placed in the hands of a receiver. If the harbour of Quebec were given the same treatment financially that has been accorded to other harbours, the figures would be quite different. Lastly, I have no doubt that the government will be quite satisfied to give to all members of the house any necessary information they may require as to the nature and character of the work which ought to be carried out at Quebec.
The Solicitor General, in coming to the rescue of tihe Minister of Marine-
I did not; he does not need any help.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Nobody is in danger on this side.

The minister gave a statement as to the amount of money guaranteed by the port of Quebec to the Dominion of Canada, but that was not a reply to my question. The figures to which I referred were the amounts supposedly owing by various departments of this government to the port of Quebec. I mentioned two, the Department of Immigration and the Department of the Interior, and in both cases the interest exceeds the principaJl of the amount claimed. I asked the minister if he could give us the number of years during which interest has been accruing, and if it was calculated at simple or compound interest.

Quebec Harbour Commission

I am not in a position to say whether it is simple or compound interest, but so far as the length of the account is concerned, it is a very old one. The first one which was produced dates back thirty years.
What was the amount of the liabilities charged up to the commission when it was first formed in 1913?
I have not that information here, but I can have it when we go into committee on the bill.
Perhaps the minister would also bring down the information I asked for.

I was very much interested in the remarks of the Solicitor General. In my judgment, all the ports that are under the administration of the commission should be on the same basis and be treated in the same way, and if it can be shown to this committee that the port of Quebec did not have as good a deal as the other ports when its commission was first formed, then I maintain that a proper settlement should be made before we go further with this legislation, so that we may know just exactly where we stand. That is a very strong reason, in my opinion, why this matter should go to a committee. If the remarks of the Solicitor General are correct, and I have no reason to doubt but that they are, I can quite understand that the people of Quebec feel they have a very strong grievance. This is the first time I have heard that this commission was charged, when it was formed, with these liabilities, and I think I am safe in saying that the committee as a whole did not understand that that was the situation. Would it be possible to prevail upon the government to clean this matter up before we go further with this legislation? I would like to see that done, and if the claims of the commission for further assistance can be shown to be well grounded, I would be satisfied.

I understand that there is a claim of 12,000,000 against the Immigration department by the port of Quebec. We have immigrants coming in also at Halifax, Montreal, Vancouver and Toronto. Is there any reason why Quebec should receive consideration in regard to these claims any more than these other ports?

There is no particular
reason except that the harbour commission of Quebec claim that the immigration causes such a tax upon their facilities as to deprive the commission of one of the best sections of 56103-140
the harbour, and they feel that they are entitled to compensation. If a similar situation exists in any other port, I would see no objection to considering the claim of that port.
Is that a valid, subsisting claim which is recognized by the government as a material, substantial claim?

So far as my department
and .myself are concerned, we are prepared to recognize that claim, but up to the present time it has not been entertained by the various departments concerned.

As long ago as 1922 when the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the present Minister of Justice, was asking for $1,500,000, he said in regard to this claim:
Of course, there is a bill standing in the books of the commission against the federal government on that account. This bill has never been paid, and I do not expect that it ever will be.
It seems to me that too much has been made of this claim. Away back in 1922 the claim was stale and was not recognized as a claim that the government would ever undertake to pay. It has dragged along for nearly six years, and after such a period an ordinary debt would be outlawed, but we find this claim now set up as an important reason why the Quebec harbour commissioners should receive consideration. There is every reason why they should receive consideration, but this is not one of them. Nor do the remarks of the Solicitor General apply, for a reference to Hansard of May 5, 1922, will show that the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries recognized that the harbour commission of Quebec was insolvent and could not pay its interest, but in course of time he hoped that it might approach to the success of the harbour commission of Montreal. We are sorry that that has not come about. But it is not on any sectional grounds as the Solicitor General alleged-
I never alleged anything of the kind. On the contrary-
Read Hansard to-morrow.
I rise to a point of order -to a question of privilege. I was particular to state my position with great care, and my hon. friend has no right to make such a statement. I deny it.

Mr. Chairman; on the point of order-



Quebec Harbour Commission
It is not a point of order; it is a question of privilege and is not debatable.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member cannot escape his responsibility. He rose to a point of order, not to a question of privilege. On the point of order I wish to say that in my hearing the hon. gentleman did refer to hon. members on this side of the house and told them to remember that Canada did not begin or end at the boundaries of Ontario. If that was not an imputation of sectionalism I do not know what is.
That may have been only a lesson in geography.
The Solicitor General also said that this was not the narrow question that the opposition were trying to make it appear.
I did not say that.

Read Hansard to-morrow. I maintain that it is not a narrow question. But the people of Canada will demand that this money when expended shall not only come under review by auditors who may be sent to the port of Quebec to examine the accounts, but by auditors who are responsible to parliament; that parliament shall have an opportunity of investigating expenditures running into millions of dollars in the case of a harbour commission which, up to the present time, has failed to carry on the business of the harbour of Quebec with success to the city and to Canada.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior

speechtext:
I may tell my hon.
friend that it was not the city, it was the parliament of Canada that inflicted this upon us.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: You should have resisted. In reply to my hon. friend from East Toronto, the Minister of Finance assured him that the very accounting that he is calling for is made to-day, notwithstanding the fact that the expenditure is under the control of the harbour commission.

I did not understand
it that way. There is no investigation by parliament into the expenditures on the harbour of Quebec; there would be in the case of any other harbours receiving money directly from the government, such as Fort William and Toronto.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If I understood my colleague correctly, he said the audit, was exactly the same as in the port of Montreal, that we would have access to the report and that full information would be given to the house.
But the point is, there would not be an investigation by the public accounts committee.

At Fort William, for
example, where there is no harbour commission, the work is done by the Public Works department under the direction of the deputy minister and his engineers, so it is done directly under the authority of the parliament

Quebec Harbour Commission
of Canada; whereas in the case of a harbour commission the work is done under their own engineer and not under the supervision of the Public Works department.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They are under the
Marine department.
The harbour is not under the Marine department.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
You are speaking of
those under commissions; they are under the Marine department.

But they have no investigatory powers. They might be able to do it if they insisted. But take any work that is done at Fort William or Port Arthur: it has to be submitted to the Public Works department, and as a matter of fact it is done by them through their own engineers and officers. They lay out the plans and perhaps call for the tenders and supervise the whole work. That is the whole difference.

When I spoke yesterday I thought the debate would close within a few minutes, but twenty-four hours have elapsed and we are still discussing this question. I suggested then, and I still contend, that if this government owes the Quebec harbour commission any money on any account the matter should be straightened out. It is unfortunate that members of the government should try to create an impression in the country that we are endeavouring to discriminate against Quebec merely because it is Quebec. There is no intention on the part of any member on this side to vote against any legal improvements or developments which may be necessary at that port. I do not think anybody wishes to take that position and it is wrong for any hon. member to insinuate anything of the kind. But we do wish to get all the details in connection with this matter and to know what is being done with the money. We are being asked to vote a large sum, and it is important that we should know just how it will be spent. If the government will give us the necessary information they will not encounter any difficulty.

I must crave the indulgence of my impatient friends opposite for speaking so late. I have been present the greater part of the two days during which this discussion has been in progress, and I have listened patiently-sometimes impatiently-in the hope of getting some information which would really justify the committee in passing the reoslution. I have been reminded of a story I once heard-
56103-140J
Oh, oh!
Get down to business.
A bedtime story? It is halfpast ten.

This story is about a coloured gentleman, a darkey who was driving a team of mules through a southern swamp. It was late in the day, and by the time he got into the interior of the swamp it was quite dark.

There was no
swamp.

A thunderstorm came up
and every time there was a flash of lightning it lit up the road. The darkey liked that, but very soon the flash was followed by a clap of thunder which naturally made the mules very restive. As the storm got worse, after a particularly brilliant flash of lightning and the resultant clap of thunder, the mules became altogether unmanageable and ran away with the darkey, who fell into the bottom of the wagon. In this plight he began to pray, and his first words as reported were these: "Oh Lord, if it's all the same to you, could we have a little less noise and more light?'' Now I think we have had the noise, but I do not believe we have had all the light that we should have had.
What about the mules?

They are
all over on the front benches.

I could not help thinking, as the minister was complaining of our having wasted two days on this question, that if we had been given the information to which I think the house is entitled when it is asked to vote $8,500,000, we might have disposed of the matter yesterday. If this question were referred to a committee and they devoted two sessions to it, I fancy they would find out all the facts by the end of that time. As it
is,	although we have spent nearly two days on
it,	we have not nearly all the information which should be given us. Perhaps it is not fair to lay all the blame on the minister, although he might have given a complete statement at the outset and so have saved a lot of time. I want to refer first of all to the question of the audit of moneys spent not only on this harbour but on all harbour commissions. That expenditure should be audited by the Auditor General's department. It is all very well for the Minister of Finance to say that he will have the audit board audit the accounts if necessary, but I have never known the audit board's reports to be submitted to parliament. The Auditor General's

Quebec Harbour Commission
report is submitted to us annually and referred to the public accounts committee, and the house has an opportunity then of finding out how every dollar is spent in every department of government. But we cannot find out anything about the expenditures of these commissions.
Oh, oh.

I regret that the one who
speaks last in these debates is under so serious a disadvantage. The house gets so noisy that it is almost impossible to speak. I do not think it is fair. I have sat and listened quietly to the discussion for two days, and now I have a right to be heard. I want to say first of all to the minister-and I do not intend to keep the committee very long-
A good thing.

Maybe, but I could talk for
half an hour if absolutely necessary. I was going to say, we voted $5,000,000 for the Quebec harbour in 1925, and we were told then that this was sufficient for a period of five years. Now after three years the minister comes back and asks for $S,500,000 more. He has not yet enlightened us as to what has made him change his mind, and why he now finds it necessary, two years before the expiry of the five-year period, to ask for this large additional vote. The minister should know just what claims ought to be allowed which are now being pressed by the commission. He might have told us what revenue has been collected by the commission during the past two years.
He did; it is all in Hansard.

Well, that must have been
while I was called out of the house. I am sorry I missed it. Somebody suggests that it is so small I did not miss very much anyway.

The light was shining,
but you weren't here to see it.

The minister might tell us- in fact, I hope he will when he brings down the bill-just how many berths there will be when he gets the wharf completed, and how many berths will be available for use. He might also let us know whether the prospective tonnage will require this additional accommodation.
Now, a word or two in regard to the proposal to erect the new storage elevator. I do not think the minister has yet given any reply to the question asked by the hon. member for
'Mr. Coote.]
Acadia as to how he was going to secure sufficient revenue from that elevator to pay interest on the' money. I did intend to read some of the remarks made by some of the hon. members in 1925 with regard to the possibility of shipping western grain through the port of Quebec, but I do not think I will do so. If anyone is interested he will find these statements reported in Hansard. The remarks of the hon. member for Provencher were particularly well put. He pointed out that in his opinion grain never would go through the port of Quebec during the open season, because the railway companies would not furnish enough cars to carry grain that distance when they could unload their cars at Fort William. In order to provide additional rolling stock which would be necessary they would have to spend millions of dollars, as the hon. member pointed out. If the hour were not so late and if some hon. members were not so impatient-and I really do not want to get into their bad graces- I would read some of the words of the hon. member.

Perhaps those gentlemen
have seen the light.

They have not seen much
light if I correctly understood the number of bushels which have been handled through the present elevator at Quebec. In my opinion we are just as likely to handle 40,000,000 bushels through that elevator in one year as the proverbial camel is to go through the eye of a needle. It never will be done, for the simple reason that grain will not go to Quebec to any extent except when the river is frozen up. Then it will be used for winter storage, and the elevator will not handle very much more than three or four times its capacity in any year.
I think the cost of elevator construction, which was given by the minister as approximately 95 cents a bushel, is much too high. It seems to me that that statement Is a sufficient reason for us to ask the government to give this question very careful consideration. In the face of the present situation, and in order to remove any doubt as to the voting of this amount the government have only to convince the house that this work is needed, I do not see why they have not been wiling to let this matter go before a small committee, preferably the public accounts committee, before which the engineers could appear and demonstrate the need for this additional accommodation at Quebec harbour.

Chicago Drainage Canal

On division.

Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Cardin thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 214, to provide for a loan to the Quebec harbour commissioners.

subtopic: PAPERS TABLED RESPECTING DIVERSION OF WATER

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: PAPERS TABLED RESPECTING DIVERSION OF WATER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would ask the
